chunks: Informed me thereof the Sheikh — may Allah have mercy on him — from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yasin al-Darir, from Hariz ibn 'Abd Allah, from Abu Basir, from Abu 'Abd Allah (AS):

that he was asked about stagnant water (al-mā' al-naqī') in which animals urinate. He said: If the water has changed, do not perform wudu from it; but if their urine has not changed it, then perform wudu from it. Likewise blood, when it flows into water, and its similars.

key_terms.الدَّوَابُّ: beasts; animals (particularly riding or pack animals)
key_terms.النَّقِيعِ: stagnant/pooled water — water that has been left standing undisturbed
key_terms.تَغَيَّرَ: changed (in qualifying properties — color, smell, or taste)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling in Shia Islam on performing wudu from stagnant water in which animals have urinated?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) was asked about standing water (al-mā' al-naqī') in which animals urinate and established the foundational jurisprudential criterion: if the water's properties (color, smell, or taste) are altered by the urine, wudu from it is prohibited; if the properties remain unchanged, wudu is valid. The Imam then extends the same criterion by analogy to blood flowing into water and similar impurities, affirming that in Shia fiqh the standard for rendering water impure is qualitative change, not the mere presence of a najis substance.
